sentences.text: Panderichthys was a lobe-finned fish that lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 380 million years ago.
Estimates of its size vary, with some sources stating it measured between 1.5 and 2 meters in length, while others suggest a range of 90 to 130 centimeters.
The animal possessed a large head similar to that of tetrapods.
Its vertebral column was fully ossified with vertebrae comparable to those of early tetrapods.
Although it had a tetrapod-like head shape, it retained an intracranial joint characteristic of fish.
The small, finger-like bones in Panderichthys lack muscle development and joints, representing an intermediate form between fish fins and tetrapod limbs.
The humerus of Panderichthys exhibits a mix of both primitive and derived anatomical features.
Researchers suggest Panderichthys may have been able to prop up its large head, a capability that probably aided in breathing.
It is hypothesized that Panderichthys used its pectoral fins to anchor itself while moving forward via side-to-side body undulation.
Panderichthys shares ten specific anatomical features with tetrapods, including a flat skull roof, paired frontals, no external intracranial joint, and complex polyplocodont teeth.
The animal is considered at least a facultative air breather, representing an intermediate stage in the evolution of air breathing.
It is considered the closest evolutionary relative to tetrapods that still possessed fins.
Fossils of Panderichthys were recovered from Frasnian deposits in Latvia.
The type species Panderichthys rhombolepis was found in Lode, Latvia.
The species Panderichthys rhombolepis was discovered by Gross in 1930, while Panderichthys stolbovi was discovered and illustrated by Emilia Vorobyeva in 1960.
The genus Panderichthys is named after the paleontologist Christian Heinrich Pander.
The genus Panderichthys was described by Gross in 1941.
It is hypothesized that P. rhombolepis was a large predator feeding on dipterids, small and juvenile sarcopterygians, and Latvius.
Due to its size and co-occurrence with bite-marked heterostracans, Panderichthys may have been a major predator of these armored jawless fish.
Panderichthys is hypothesized to have been adapted for moving in shallow, debris-filled waters in a marginal marine environment.
Analysis of the humerus suggests that the evolutionary transition from fish-like limb structures to tetrapod limbs occurred more slowly than previously thought.
The discovery of possible tetrapod tracks predating Panderichthys suggests that the genus was not a direct ancestor of tetrapods.
The genus Panderichthys includes the species Panderichthys stolbovi (described by Vorobyeva in 1960) and Panderichthys rhombolepis (described by Gross in 1941).
Its parent group is the family Panderichthyidae.
It is classified within the class Osteichthyes.
Recent studies redefine Elpistostegalia as a clade starting with Panderichthys and including all living tetrapods.
Shultze and Arsenault were the first researchers in 1985 to recognize that Panderichthys was phylogenetically closer to tetrapods than to fish.
